title: Observability, SLOs and error budgets
subtitle: Logs, metrics and traces show what your system does. SLOs and error budgets tell you when to act.

c.v: Meera's team runs the checkout API for an online shop. Their dashboard has 40 graphs. On Tuesday evening, every graph looks fine. Average
latency
is 120 ms. CPU is at 45%.
At the same time, one in ten customers cannot pay. A new release broke payments for one card type. Those requests
fail fast
, so they even pull the average latency down.
Nobody is paged. The team gets 200 alerts a week about CPU and disk, so they have learned to ignore the alert channel. The problem is found the next morning, from angry messages to support.
The team had a lot of data, but no clear answer to one question:
"Are our users getting what they need right now?"
(This story is made up, but the pattern is common.)
Observability

means you can understand what your system is doing from the data it sends out. Most of that data comes in three kinds. OpenTelemetry lists these three, plus other signals such as baggage, which carries context between them
Metrics
numbers measured over time, like requests per second or error rate. Cheap to keep, good for graphs and alerts.
Logs:
a record of one event, like "payment 7f3a failed: card declined". Rich in detail, but large.
Traces
the path of one request through many services. A trace is made of
spans
, one for each step, with its timing.
Data alone does not tell you when to act. For that you need a target that matches what users feel:
An
SLI
(service level indicator) is a measure of service, best written as
good events ÷ total events
. In practice, count only valid events: leave out calls like
health checks
. For example: the share of checkout requests that succeed in under 500 ms.
An
SLO
(service level objective) is the target for that SLI over a time window. For example: 99.9% over a rolling 4 weeks
. The alerting maths below uses a 30-day window instead, as the alerting chapter does
An
SLA
(service level agreement) is a contract with customers that has a penalty, often money, if you miss it
The
error budget
is the part you are allowed to fail: 100% minus the SLO
. With a 99.9% SLO and 1 million requests, you can fail 1,000 of them.
The key idea.
Never aim for 100%. It is not realistic
. A user on a phone that works 99% of the time cannot tell 99.99% from 99.999%
. Pick a target, then spend the error budget on purpose. When some budget is left, ship. When it is gone, fix reliability first
Availability maths: the nines
Each extra "nine" cuts the allowed downtime by 10
about 7.2 hours a month.
about 43 minutes a month.
about 4.3 minutes a month.
about 26 seconds a month.

Services that depend on each other multiply. If checkout needs three services in a row, each 99.9%, the best it can do is 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 99.7%. This assumes they fail independently. Two copies in parallel help: if each copy is 99% and they really fail independently, both are down only 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.01% of the time. In real life, copies often fail together, for example after one bad config change.
What to measure
Google's SRE book suggests
four golden signals
for any service:
latency, traffic, errors and saturation
(how full the service is)
. It also warns that averages hide slow requests. A service with an average latency of 100 ms can still have 1% of requests take 5 seconds
. So use
percentiles
, like p99, in your SLIs.
Burn-rate alerts
The
burn rate
is how fast you spend the error budget, compared with the speed that would use it up exactly at the end of the window
. At burn rate 1, the budget lasts 30 days. At burn rate 10, it is gone in 3 days
Step through a bad deploy and see how a burn-rate alert reacts. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
The Site Reliability Workbook recommends three alerts for a 99.9% SLO
Page
if the burn rate is above 14.4 over the last hour
and
the last 5 minutes. That is 2% of the 30-day budget in one hour.
Page
if it is above 6 over the last 6 hours
and
the last 30 minutes. That is 5% of the budget.
Open a ticket
if it is above 1 over the last 3 days
and
the last 6 hours. That is 10% of the budget.
The long window proves the problem is real. The short window makes the alert stop a few minutes after the problem stops
Alert on causes (CPU, disk, memory)
Users can suffer while CPU is fine.
High. Many alerts need no action.
Only as tickets or dashboards, to help find a cause.
Alert on any error
, but too early.
Very high. Every short error pages someone.
Almost never for paging.
Simple SLO threshold (error rate above 0.1% for 10 minutes)
Medium. Short spikes can still page.
A first step, while you learn your traffic.
Multiwindow, multi-burn-rate SLO alerts
Fast for big outages, slower for small, steady error rates.
Low.
Most user-facing services, once SLOs exist.
Simple rule:
page a human only for symptoms that users feel. Keep cause metrics for debugging

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Start from the user's journey: "Can a customer pay?" Write the SLI as good events ÷ valid events. Then add the SLO.
Choose the SLO with the product owner. Use past data, and do not promise more than your dependencies give you.
Write an
error budget policy
before you need it. For example: if the budget for 4 weeks is spent, stop feature launches and work on reliability until the service is back within the SLO
Put a trace ID in every log line. Then you can jump from a slow trace to the logs of that exact request.
Keep monitoring separate from what it watches. In 2021, Roblox was down for 73 hours, and its monitoring depended on Consul, the system that was failing. That slowed the team's diagnosis
. Slack's dashboards and alerts also failed in its January 2021 outage, because they reached their databases through the overloaded network
Delete or fix every alert that pages without needing action. Alert noise trains people to ignore the real alert.

"Write a Prometheus recording rule for the checkout SLI: the share of requests that return a non-5xx status in under 500 ms. Then write burn-rate alerts for a 99.9% SLO, with 1 hour and 5 minute windows at 14.4, and 6 hour and 30 minute windows at 6."
"Add OpenTelemetry tracing to this HTTP handler. Add the trace ID to every log line it writes."
The SLI counts only valid requests. Decide on purpose whether health checks and 4xx errors from bad user input count.
The burn-rate maths matches your SLO. A burn rate of 14.4 for a 99.9% SLO means an error rate of 1.44%.
Each alert uses both a long and a short window.
The latency SLI uses a percentile or a threshold count, never an average.
Logs do not contain passwords, card numbers or other personal data.
Next on this line:
Alerting and on-call
explains how to page humans only for what matters.

q.v: Your SLO is 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days. You serve 10 million requests in that time. How many failed requests can you afford?

why.v: The error budget is 100% − 99.9% = 0.1%. 0.1% of 10 million is 10,000.

q.v: What does a burn rate of 1 mean?

options.v: The error budget will run out exactly at the end of the SLO window.
One error happened in the last hour.

why.v: Burn rate compares how fast you spend the budget with the speed that would use it up exactly at the end of the window.

q.v: A checkout needs three services, one after another. Each is 99.9% available, and they fail independently. What is the best availability checkout can have?

why.v: 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.997. Every service in the chain adds its own failures.

q.v: Which alert is most likely to page on real user pain, and not on noise?

options.v: The error budget is burning 14.4 times too fast over both the last hour and the last 5 minutes.

why.v: It measures what users feel, and the two windows stop it from firing on short problems or long after the problem ends.

q.v: About how much downtime does 99.9% availability allow in a 30-day month?

why.v: 0.1% of 30 days is 43.2 minutes. Each extra nine divides the allowed downtime by 10.
